A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same four-stage control framework and three simulation tasks. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, proofs, and experimental appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original boat-navigation, pursuer–evader, and multi-agent simulations, including cost, safety, computation-time, and numerical-solver comparisons.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation results and adds PPO-Lag/CPO comparisons and empirical safety-bound validation using three million initial states.

M1.justification: The epigraph formulation, PDE and boundary losses, curriculum, network architecture, conformal algorithms, and binary-search inference remain. Section 3.1 newly specifies adaptive loss rebalancing, but does not establish that the earlier training procedure changed; this adds implementation information.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2D boat, 8D pursuer–evader, and 20D five-agent navigation tasks with the same dynamics and obstacle/goal requirements. The added calibration experiment reuses the boat setting. Removal of the six-second pursuer rollout changes the deployment protocol within an existing task.

E2.justification: v3 adds PPO-Lagrangian and Constrained Policy Optimization to the cost, safety, and runtime comparisons across all three tasks (Figures 2 and 6). C-SAC is renamed SAC-Lag, with its reward, training settings, and headline results retained. The two additional comparators substantially broaden the constrained-RL comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix B.1.2 adds validation using three million initial-state rollouts while retaining 300,000 calibration samples. New PPO-Lag/CPO experiments have documented rewards and training budgets. The six-second receding-horizon test is removed. Existing task settings and proposed-method budgets remain; computation time was already evaluated in v1 Appendix J.

E4.justification: v3 adds sample-size/confidence sensitivity analysis (Appendix A.3, Figure 7) and directly compares empirical safety violations against theoretical bounds across correction levels (Appendix B.1.2, Figure 9), substantially extending v1's calculated delta–epsilon curve. Conversely, v1's beyond-training-horizon pursuer case study and Figure 6 disappear.

E5.justification: The original experiments retain their calibration counts, confidence parameters, violation thresholds, and conformal reporting procedure. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or benchmark error bars. The new sample-size analysis and empirical validation examine existing statistical guarantees rather than introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figures 2 and 6 add PPO-Lag/CPO cost, safety, and runtime outcomes across all tasks. Figure 9 adds empirical violation rates below the theoretical bound. Online-runtime bars are revised, and Section 4.4 explicitly reports 2 ms policy computation. The six-second rollout result is removed, while original headline cost/safety summaries and delta/psi estimates remain.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 changes its stated guarantee from the induced-policy rollout value to the optimal auxiliary value. Appendix A.1 retains the rollout bound and adds the inequality linking these values to derive the revised conclusion. Section 2.2 also explicitly conditions the viscosity-solution characterization on Altarovici et al.'s assumptions A1–A4; the remaining mathematical framework is largely retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: scalable safety/performance co-optimization through physics-informed epigraph learning, conformal safety verification, and probabilistic performance-error bounds, demonstrated on three case studies. Added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 adds substantive discussion of calibration variability and the sample-size/confidence/conservatism tradeoff. Section 4.4 attributes favorable runtime scaling to neural-network parallelization. The interpretation that short-horizon training supports longer receding-horizon deployment is removed, while baseline limitations are extended to the additional CRL methods.

D1.justification: v3 adds PPO-Lag/CPO reward equations and configuration tables, discloses adaptive loss rebalancing, and provides a project-site reference for trajectory visualizations. Existing hardware, network, and original baseline settings are retained. These extend implementation documentation without replacing the reproducibility information already present in v1.

R1.justification: The introduction adds discussion of restricted-system HJB solvers and explicitly contrasts the approach with safety-only DeepReach. Additional references cover PINNs, safety filtering, safe-RL infrastructure, and adaptive loss balancing; the Haarnoja SAC reference is removed. The central positioning around epigraph-based safety/performance co-optimization remains.

P1.justification: Most core prose is retained, with targeted contextual additions and C-SAC renamed SAC-Lag. Computation-time discussion moves into Section 4.4, and the former Appendices A–K are grouped into proofs, system details, and implementation details with a contents page. Acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICML layout, expands and recolors comparison charts, moves the runtime chart into the main text, adds the sample-size plot and two configuration tables, and expands the calibration plot with empirical results and another axis. Several trajectory/heatmap illustrations are redrawn, theorem statements are boxed in the appendix, and the receding-horizon figure is removed.

improvement.justification: Additional constrained-RL comparisons and the three-million-state safety-bound check strengthen empirical scrutiny, while the calibration discussion improves interpretation. These benefits are moderated by removal of the six-second deployment example and incomplete reconciliation of the expanded comparisons: Section 4.1 still calls SAC-Lag the least safe baseline although Figure 2 shows PPO-Lag lower. Overall, the evidence supports a limited quality gain.
